title: Capacity warmup and temporary node-bridge runbook (prototype)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working prototype runbook describing a "temporary node-bridge" pattern plus capacity warmup steps to handle GPU node maintenance / replacements without violating latency SLOs. The idea: bring an isolated set of warm nodes (bridge) into the cluster, migrate traffic with controlled ramp, warm model caches, then perform GPU replacement/cordon/drain on target machines. This doc focuses on operational steps, verification queries, backout criteria, and post-incident notes.

When to use:
- Planned maintenance when we expect to drain > 20% of GPU capacity in a zone.
- Emergency hot-swap when an accelerator shows intermittent ECC or driver OOMs and we need a fast evacuation path.
- Short-term capacity spike where autoscaler cannot provision identical GPU instances fast enough.

Assumptions and prerequisites:
- Private/shared pool available in the same region with compatible GPU types (or lower-cap variant with quantized models).
- Deployment manifests support nodeSelector / tolerations for bridge nodes.
- Model-serving jobs support prefix-KV warming (cache restore) and can be started with batch=1 to quickly populate KV cache.
- Monitoring dashboards (Prometheus/Grafana) reachable and alerting silences editable.
- Slack channel #sre-oncall and #infra-ops are monitored; runbook owner can escalate to oncall lead.

Key safety signals (pre-flight checks):
- Current cluster GPU utilization and free capacity: PromQL: sum(gpu_memory_used_bytes) / sum(gpu_memory_total_bytes) by (zone)
- Request latency P95/P99 for top 5 routes: redwood_api_request_duration_seconds{route=~"/v1/(chat|completions|embedding).*"}
- Model queue length / in-flight requests: redwood_model_queue_depth{model!=""}
- Active autoscaler activity: inspect autoscaler events: kubectl -n infra get hpa,podautoscaler -o wide

Runbook (step-by-step prototype):
1) Notify stakeholders (5–10m)
   - Post an intent message in #sre-oncall and #prod-alerts: short plan, ETA, rollback window.
   - Create ephemeral incident channel #inc-capacity-warmup-<yyyymmdd>.

2) Provision bridge nodes (10–25m depending on cloud)
   - Acquire nodes from Reserved pool or spin new instances via infra repo (pref: same image + runtime).
   - Label nodes: kubectl label node <node-name> role=bridge-capacity --overwrite
   - Tolerations/taints: apply taint to bridge nodes to ensure only warmup pods land: kubectl taint nodes <node> bridge=true:NoSchedule
   - Confirm kubectl get nodes -l role=bridge-capacity -o wide shows new nodes Ready.

3) Deploy warmup DaemonSet / Job (5–15m)
   - Purpose: start minimal model-serving pods that will load model weights into GPU memory and populate prefix/KV caches so cold-start latency is avoided when traffic is shifted.
   - Example steps:
       * Apply warmup job: kubectl apply -f ops/bridge/warmup-job.yaml (job runs model init scripts)
       * Warmup config: start with batch_size=1, max_seq=128, concurrency=2 to load weights with low overhead.
   - Verification: watch GPU memory and model init logs: kubectl -n models logs -l job=bridge-warmup -f

4) Soft traffic shift (ramp, 15–40m)
   - Strategy A: Router weight shift (preferred for hosted API): adjust routing policy to send 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% to bridge over 5–10 minute intervals while observing latency and error budget.
   - Strategy B: K8s service split: create canary service with subset selectors and flip weights in the load balancer.
   - Traffic ramp checklist:
       * After each step wait 5m and verify P95 < SLO threshold + 10% and error rate <= baseline * 2.
       * Monitor model-specific metrics: kv_cache_hit_ratio, gpu_utilization by pod.

5) Drain original nodes (cordon & drain)
   - Mark node unschedulable: kubectl cordon <node>
   - Drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=15m
   - If pod stuck: describe pod to see eviction blockers: kubectl -n <ns> describe pod <pod> and check PVCs/hostPath. If PVCs block, follow PVC migration pattern (see linked confluence).
   - If eviction fails: fallback to route-level fallback (send traffic away from model/version) and escalate to hardware oncall.

6) Physical GPU replacement / node repair
   - Follow hardware vendor guide. High-level sequence: power down, hot-swap accelerator, verify firmware, boot and run smoke tests (nvidia-smi, driver version, mig config if applicable).
   - Post-swap: bring node Ready, re-label and remove taint: kubectl label node <node> role=serving-gpu --overwrite; kubectl taint node <node> bridge=true:NoSchedule-

7) Rebalance traffic back (reverse warmdown)
   - Prefer gradual traffic return: 10% -> 50% -> 100% while observing errors/latency for 5–10 minutes per step.
   - If bridge used cheaper/smaller GPUs with quantized models, migrate models back to original nodes only after validating quality metrics (tox tests / eval harness).

Verification and metrics to track during operation:
- P95 / P99 latency for impacted routes and model-specific tail latencies.
- Token throughput and tokens/s per GPU.
- KV cache hit ratio: aim for >= 80% on warmed models.
- Error rate (5xx / 429): should not exceed baseline * 2.
- Node GPU free memory and temperature (watch for thermal events after swap).

Backout criteria (when to abort and rollback immediately):
- P99 > SLO * 1.5 for > 10 minutes.
- Sustained error rate > 3x baseline or new uncaught 5xx spike.
- Bridge nodes failing to reach GPU init state (nvidia-smi errors, driver mismatches).
- Critical dependent service starts to queue requests beyond acceptable threshold.
If any backout criteria hit: immediately shift traffic to unaffected region / fallback model variant and document incident.

Common troubleshooting notes and commands:
- Check pod GPU allocation: kubectl -n models get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GPU:.metadata.annotations -l app=model-serving
- Inspect GPU errors: kubectl -n kube-system logs -l app=kubelet -f | grep -i nvidia
- Force-evict trick (last resort): kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=0 --force (use only if drained node blocks recovery)
- Inspect mounting blockers: kubectl describe pod <pod> and look for MountVolume.WaitForAttach errors

Cost & billing note:
- Bridge nodes incur transient cost; prefer using pooled reserved capacity or spot instances with fallback to reserved. Track billing tag: tag/incident=<inc-id>.

Post-incident checklist (to be completed within 72h):
- Root cause summary and timeline (owner: Aisha Patel).
- Confirm all bridge nodes returned to normal pool or decommissioned.
- Run synthetic evals comparing outputs before/after if quantized models were used.
- File follow-ups: infra automation to make warmup jobs parameterized (PR: infra#bridge-warmup-params).
- Update runbook with lessons learned and add automation steps for 1-click bridge provisioning.

Open TODOs (prototype work items):
- [ ] Add automated traffic ramp script tied to observation windows.
- [ ] Build warmup job image with configurable model list and KV restore.
- [ ] Add Grafana panel template for bridge operation view.
- [ ] Document PCI/KMS considerations when moving models to bridge nodes in private deployments.

Notes to self (informal):
- When we first tested, 2x small-bridge nodes warmed 4 models in ~6m; kv hit ratio hit 75% after 3 mins. Good baseline for future.
- Watch out for driver micro-version mismatches — they silently cause GPU init to fail and pods crash-loop.
- Consider making model-serving init logs more explicit: emit "KV_CACHE_READY" marker so automation can detect readiness instead of heuristics.

References and related playbooks:
- confluence:gpu-maintenance-playbook-v2 (detailed hardware swap steps)
- infra runbook: node-evacuate-pvc-migration (PVC migration for stateful pods)
- Jira INFRA-2145: bridge prototype experiments and test results

Appendix: quick command snippets
- Label nodes as bridge:
  kubectl label node <node> role=bridge-capacity --overwrite
- Taint bridge node (prevent general scheduling):
  kubectl taint node <node> bridge=true:NoSchedule
- Start warmup job (example):
  kubectl -n models apply -f ops/bridge/bridge-warmup-job.yaml
- Graceful drain with timeout:
  kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=15m

End of prototype.
If you run this, add a short incident note with timestamps and outcome in the linked Jira ticket.
